Exporting and reporting results

Justin Chase

Source: vignettes/reporting.Rmd
reporting.Rmd

This article covers what leaves your session once the cells and the model are settled: the cells as a file, the values in them, the model’s score with the checks that bound it, and what to save to rerun the analysis.

This article needs two optional packages: ggplot2 for the map and gstat for the autocorrelation range. Where one is missing, the code that needs it is shown but not run.

The cells as a file someone else can use

The example is North Carolina’s counties, with the 1974 SIDS rate per 1,000 births, and hexagonal cells laid over the county centres rather than the county boundaries.

library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
counties <- ensure_projected(nc[, c("NAME", "BIR74", "SID74")])
counties$rate <- 1000 * counties$SID74 / counties$BIR74

centres  <- coerce_to_points(counties)
boundary <- clip_target_for(centres, expand = 0.01)
hex      <- build_tessellation(centres, method = "hex", approx_n_cells = 12,
                               boundary = boundary)$cells
nrow(hex)
## [1] 17

The boundary is the bounding box of the county centres, grown by 1 percent of its longer side (clip_target_for()). Hexagons over it came out at 17 for a request of 12, so quote the count that comes back.

Each county goes to the cell it overlaps most (largest = TRUE, which vignette("cells") explains), and summarize_by_cell() reduces the counties to one row per cell. Passing cells_sf keeps the geometry, and keeps the cells that hold no county with NA values.

grouped <- assign_features_to_polygons(counties, hex,
                                       polygon_id_col = "cell_id",
                                       largest = TRUE)
cells <- summarize_by_cell(grouped, response_var = "rate", id_col = "cell_id",
                           cells_sf = hex, conf_level = 0.95)
names(cells)
##  [1] "cell_id"                   "n"                        
##  [3] "resp_mean_rate"            "..sd_resp_rate"           
##  [5] "..se_resp_rate"            "..neff_resp_rate"         
##  [7] "..df_resp_rate"            "..ci_lo_resp_rate"        
##  [9] "..ci_hi_resp_rate"         "cell_weight"              
## [11] "..pooled_resp_rate"        "..pooled_w_resp_rate"     
## [13] "..pooled_target_resp_rate" "geometry"

The box also covers ground outside the state, with no county centre, so 5 of the 17 cells hold no county. With the state outline as boundary, the same request gives 12 cells, none of them empty.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = cells, aes(fill = resp_mean_rate), colour = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = counties, fill = NA, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "SIDS rate\nper 1,000", na.value = "grey92") +
  labs(title = "Counties grouped into hexagonal cells",
       subtitle = sprintf("%d cells, %d with a county; grey = no county inside",
                          nrow(cells), sum(!is.na(cells$n)))) +
  theme_void()

Is this location inside?

Someone holding the cells may want to know whether a new location falls in one. assign_features_to_polygons() with keep_unassigned = TRUE answers that: it returns one row per location, with NA for a location outside every cell.

sites <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(site = c("Raleigh", "Wilmington", "Atlantic", "Norfolk VA"),
             lon  = c(-78.64, -77.95, -74.50, -76.29),
             lat  = c( 35.78,  34.23,  35.00,  36.85)),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

inside <- assign_features_to_polygons(sites, cells, polygon_id_col = "cell_id",
                                      keep_unassigned = TRUE)
st_drop_geometry(inside)
##         site cell_id
## 1    Raleigh      12
## 2 Wilmington      13
## 3   Atlantic      NA
## 4 Norfolk VA      NA

2 of the 4 sites fall inside a cell. The default, keep_unassigned = FALSE, drops the locations outside every cell, with a warning, and lists their rows in attr(, "unassigned")$which. That suits aggregation. For a membership question keep them, so the answer has one row per location you asked about.

The sites can stay in lon/lat. assign_features_to_polygons() moves them into the cells’ CRS for the join and returns them in the CRS they arrived in. A point on a border two cells share falls in both, and tie_break decides which one it is recorded in; ?assign_features_to_polygons gives the rules.

IDs that survive a reprojection

The cell_id a tessellation carries is already derived from the geometry, so it does not change when the input points arrive in another order. ensure_stable_poly_id() sorts the cells by the centroid of each, measured in longitude and latitude, and numbers them in that order. Anyone who runs it on the same set of cells gets the same IDs, whatever projection their copy is in, even without your cell_id column. Add or remove a cell and the numbers after it shift. Fine cells stacked within about a centimetre of the same longitude can swap (see ?ensure_stable_poly_id); cells this size are nowhere near that.

hex$src <- seq_len(nrow(hex))

from_projected <- ensure_stable_poly_id(hex[, "src"])
from_lonlat    <- ensure_stable_poly_id(st_transform(hex[, "src"], 4326))

identical(from_projected$poly_id[order(from_projected$src)],
          from_lonlat$poly_id[order(from_lonlat$src)])
## [1] TRUE

Join on the poly_id column that ensure_stable_poly_id() adds, not on the row position.

Writing it out

The cells are an ordinary sf layer, so sf::st_write() writes them; the format decides which columns come back intact. The layer written here carries the stable IDs:

dir <- tempfile()
dir.create(dir)
out <- ensure_stable_poly_id(cells)

st_write(out, file.path(dir, "cells.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
gpkg <- st_read(file.path(dir, "cells.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)

st_write(out, file.path(dir, "cells.shp"), quiet = TRUE)
shp <- st_read(file.path(dir, "cells.shp"), quiet = TRUE)

attr_names <- function(x) setdiff(names(x), attr(x, "sf_column"))
same_name  <- function(x) intersect(attr_names(x), attr_names(out))

c(columns = length(attr_names(out)),
  GeoPackage = length(same_name(gpkg)), shapefile = length(same_name(shp)))
##    columns GeoPackage  shapefile 
##         14         14          3
attr_names(shp)
##  [1] "cell_id"    "n"          "rsp_mn_"    "X__sd_r_"   "X__s_rs_"  
##  [6] "X__nff__"   "X__df_r_"   "X__c_l__"   "X__c_h__"   "cll_wgh"   
## [11] "X__pld__"   "X__pld_w__" "X__pld_t__" "poly_id"

A shapefile field name is capped at ten characters. Of the 14 columns, only cell_id, n and poly_id keep their names. The rest come back abbreviated: the cell mean resp_mean_rate as rsp_mn_, its standard error as X__s_rs_ and the pooled value as X__pld__. The GeoPackage keeps every column under its own name and renames only the geometry column, a GeoPackage convention. Write a GeoPackage unless something downstream reads only shapefiles. For a shapefile, choose the short names yourself and save the list of them beside it:

short <- c(mean   = "resp_mean_rate",     se     = "..se_resp_rate",
           ci_lo  = "..ci_lo_resp_rate",  ci_hi  = "..ci_hi_resp_rate",
           pooled = "..pooled_resp_rate", pool_w = "..pooled_w_resp_rate")
for_shp <- out[, c("poly_id", "cell_id", "n", short)]
names(for_shp)[match(short, names(for_shp))] <- names(short)

st_write(for_shp, file.path(dir, "cells-short.shp"), quiet = TRUE)
write.csv(data.frame(field = names(short), column = short),
          file.path(dir, "cells-short-fields.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

Reporting a cell mean

Report the standard error that summarize_by_cell() gives beside each cell mean, with the count n. A mean of a few observations and a mean of many are different claims, and printed side by side they look the same.

populated <- cells[!is.na(cells$n), ]
range(populated$n)
## [1]  2 13
range(populated$..se_resp_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
## [1] 0.1616037 0.6601569

Here the cells hold 2 to 13 counties, and their standard errors run from 0.16 to 0.66 per 1,000 births. For a cell’s own mean, the default deff = 1 standard error holds when the cell’s observations are spread through it. Any other deff ("kish", "variogram" or a number above 1) gives the standard error of the cell mean as an estimate of the statewide mean. vignette("cells") explains the difference, and ?summarize_by_cell gives the rules.

Reporting a pooled cell value

summarize_by_cell() returns by default, beside each cell’s mean, a pooled value: the cell’s mean pulled toward the mean of the observations in the 8 nearest cells (nearest by the centroid of their observations). This section builds cells sized for that value on a simulated layer and reads off what a report of them has to carry. The layer is 600 points on a square 20 km on a side, with a smooth field plus noise:

set.seed(7)
sx <- runif(600, 0, 2e4)
sy <- runif(600, 0, 2e4)
obs <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 4e5 + sx, y = 4e6 + sy,
             yield = 50 + 6 * sin(sx / 3000) + 6 * cos(sy / 2500) +
               rnorm(600, sd = 3)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32617)

By default resolution_profile() sets the count from a size of 4.5 observations per cell, scores it for the pooled value and draws density-weighted cells; the calls below leave all three at their defaults. get_voronoi_seeds() given the selection returns the centres that were scored, so the summary describes the same cells.

prof  <- resolution_profile(obs, "yield")
sel   <- select_resolution(prof)
seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(n = sel, sample_points = obs)
tess  <- build_tessellation(seeds, method = "voronoi", quiet = TRUE)
asg   <- assign_features_to_polygons(obs, tess$cells,
                                     polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
vals  <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "yield", id_col = "cell_id",
                           cells_sf = tess$cells, obs_level = 0.90)

st_drop_geometry(vals)[1:4, c("cell_id", "n", "resp_mean_yield",
                              "..pooled_resp_yield", "..pooled_w_resp_yield",
                              "..obs_lo_resp_yield", "..obs_hi_resp_yield")]
##   cell_id n resp_mean_yield ..pooled_resp_yield ..pooled_w_resp_yield
## 1       1 5        47.02646            48.21422             0.5948201
## 2       2 3        53.30889            55.94499             0.4683181
## 3       3 5        55.26101            56.30355             0.5948201
## 4       4 4        51.52654            51.46519             0.5401097
##   ..obs_lo_resp_yield ..obs_hi_resp_yield
## 1            42.54607            53.63585
## 2            50.27684            61.36662
## 3            50.63540            61.72518
## 4            45.79704            56.88682

estimate = "mean" in the summary gives the plain means alone; vignette("resolution") covers the other ways to set the count.

Three attributes of vals record the run. attr(vals, "pooled") says what was fitted and what each interval covers, attr(vals, "count_rule") how the count was set and whether these are the cells and rows it was scored on, and attr(vals, "intervals") gives one sentence per interval family:

attr(vals, "pooled")
## Cell values: yield, 600 rows in 133 cells
##   value       : ..pooled_resp_yield, pooled toward the 8 nearest cells (centroids of the rows)
##   variances   : inside cells 9.52 (from 467 values beyond one per cell);
##                 between a cell and its target 2.79
##   own weight  : median 0.54 (..pooled_w_resp_yield)
##   alone       : 0.3% of the rows are the only one in their cell
##   loo         : 10.8 (leave-one-out mean squared error of the pooled value);
##                 one mean for all rows: 42.1
##   interval    : 90% for ONE OBSERVATION (..obs_lo_resp_yield, ..obs_hi_resp_yield):
##                 value - 5.67 to value + 5.42, quantiles of 600 leave-one-out residuals
## Away from the observations no interval here is calibrated.
attr(vals, "count_rule")
## Count: 133 cells, set by size (4.5 rows per cell, the default; 600 rows / 133 cells = 4.51)
##   chosen for  : the pooled value
##   cells       : density, 3 density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8
##                 neighbours; seed 123), fitted to every row;
##                 these are the cells the profile scored
##   scored      : loo 10.8 on 600 rows in 133 cells (one cell: 42.1); 0.3% of rows alone
##   checked     : the cells and rows summarised are the ones scored

A report of cell values reads four things off them.

  • Which value it is. ..pooled_resp_yield is the pooled value and resp_mean_yield the plain mean; vignette("cells") says what both estimate. Give n beside either.
  • The own weight. ..pooled_w_resp_yield is the share of the pooled value that is the cell’s own mean, and it grows with the cell’s count. It is no regression weight: for a regression on cell values use the plain mean with cell_weight (vignette("cells")).
  • What the interval covers. ..obs_lo_* and ..obs_hi_* are a range for one further observation in the cell, located like the data. The statement holds on average over observations and not cell by cell, and the two offsets are the same in every cell. No interval for the cell’s true mean is returned. ..ci_*, from conf_level, is an interval for a mean and never a range for an observation. The table in attr(vals, "intervals") gives the sentence for each family in the frame.
  • Where the value applies. A cell’s value and interval describe the part of the cell where its observations lie, and a Voronoi cell can reach far past them. A cell with no observation has NA. Away from the observations no interval here is calibrated.

The lines of a report can be written from the three records, so that they describe the run that happened:

rec <- attr(vals, "pooled")$columns$resp_yield
iv  <- attr(vals, "intervals")
cr  <- attr(vals, "count_rule")
say <- function(...) cat(strwrap(paste0("- ", ...), width = 76, exdent = 2),
                         sep = "\n")

say(sprintf("cells: %d, set by a %s of %s observations per cell; checked: %s",
            cr$cells, cr$rule, format(cr$obs_per_cell_asked), cr$check$cells))
## - cells: 133, set by a size of 4.5 observations per cell; checked: match
say(sprintf(paste("value: the cell mean pooled toward its %d nearest cells;",
                  "median own weight %.2f"),
            rec$neighbours, rec$own_weight))
## - value: the cell mean pooled toward its 8 nearest cells; median own weight
##   0.54
say(sprintf("%s: %g%% for %s", iv$columns[1], 100 * iv$level[1], iv$covers[1]))
## - ..obs_lo_, ..obs_hi_: 90% for one further observation in the cell,
##   located like the data; on average over observations, not cell by cell
say(sprintf(paste("leave-one-out mean squared error %.3g against %.3g for one",
                  "mean; structured: %s"),
            rec$loo, rec$loo_one_cell, rec$structured))
## - leave-one-out mean squared error 10.8 against 42.1 for one mean;
##   structured: TRUE
say(sprintf("%.1f%% of observations are the only one in their cell",
            100 * rec$share_alone))
## - 0.3% of observations are the only one in their cell

structured is FALSE when one mean for the whole layer predicts a left-out observation about as well as the cells do or better, or when an F test finds the cell means no different from one mean; ?summarize_by_cell gives the thresholds, and vignette("cells") shows the warning that comes with it.

cell_values_at() gives the value at other locations with its interval. Report dist_ratio beside a value read at a place that is not an observation: the location’s distance from the nearest observation over the layer’s spacing. vignette("cells") explains the call, the seeds that extend the Voronoi cells past the clipped edge, and filled. The third location below lies outside the layer:

seeds$cell_id <- tess$index
elsewhere <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 4e5 + c(5000, 12000, 26000), y = 4e6 + c(5000, 9000, 10000)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32617)
at <- cell_values_at(elsewhere, vals, asg, "yield", id_col = "cell_id",
                     seeds = seeds)

shown <- c("cell_id", "value", "obs_lo", "obs_hi", "filled", "dist_ratio")
num   <- c("value", "obs_lo", "obs_hi", "dist_ratio")
at[num] <- lapply(at[num], round, 2)
at[, shown]
##   cell_id value obs_lo obs_hi filled dist_ratio
## 1      35 54.28  48.61  59.70  FALSE       0.65
## 2      85 39.29  33.62  44.71  FALSE       1.64
## 3     129 46.75  41.09  52.18  FALSE      15.89
outside <- at[3, ]

The third location gets a value and an interval like the others, with no warning; its dist_ratio of about 16 is what shows that it lies far from every observation. On simulated layers of clustered observations, some held out at random and some as a block, the interval at 0.90 held 91.5 percent of held-out observations with a dist_ratio below 1 and 69.5 percent of those above 8. The script is dev/sim-pooled-values.R in the package’s GitHub repository, and ?cell_values_at gives its settings and the coverage in the dist_ratio classes between those two.

Reporting a model’s score

A model to report on

The counties carry a real response, but a weak one, so this part runs on a simulated field over the same county centres. The field has an exponential covariance with range parameter 120 km, so its correlation falls to 5 percent at about 360 km, three times the range parameter.

set.seed(42)
xy    <- st_coordinates(centres)
D     <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
field <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 120e3) + diag(1e-8, nrow(D)))) %*%
                      rnorm(nrow(D)))

pts <- centres
pts$elev <- rnorm(nrow(pts))
pts$z    <- 0.8 * pts$elev + 2 * field + rnorm(nrow(pts), sd = 0.3)

The model is a linear trend surface in the coordinates plus elev, written with new_spatial_fit() so the article needs no optional package; vignette("models") explains the pattern.

trend_fit <- function(train_sf, ...) {
  d  <- st_drop_geometry(train_sf)
  co <- st_coordinates(train_sf)
  d$x <- co[, 1]; d$y <- co[, 2]
  new_spatial_fit(subclass = "trend_fit",
                  engine = stats::lm(z ~ elev + x + y, data = d),
                  formula = z ~ elev + x + y, response_var = "z",
                  predictor_vars = "elev", data_sf = train_sf)
}
predict.trend_fit <- function(object, newdata = NULL, ...) {
  if (is.null(newdata)) return(stats::fitted(object$engine))
  d  <- st_drop_geometry(newdata)
  co <- st_coordinates(newdata)
  d$x <- co[, 1]; d$y <- co[, 2]
  as.numeric(stats::predict(object$engine, newdata = d))
}
residuals.trend_fit <- function(object, ...) stats::residuals(object$engine)
fitted.trend_fit    <- function(object, ...) stats::fitted(object$engine)
# Registered so that spatialkit's own calls find the methods wherever this
# code runs; at the top level of a script they are found without it.
for (.g in c("predict", "residuals", "fitted"))
  registerS3method(.g, "trend_fit", get(paste0(.g, ".trend_fit")))

folds <- make_folds(pts, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 100e3,
                    seed = 1)
cv    <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", "elev", trend_fit, folds = folds)
fit   <- trend_fit(pts)

A worked report

Three lines of the report below are read from objects the run already made: the folds from folds, and the score and the row accounting from cv. The others come from checks run for the report: residual_morans_i() and area_of_applicability() on the fitted model and, where gstat is installed, estimate_sac_range() on the data, set beside the block size.

m <- function(x) format(round(as.numeric(x)), big.mark = ",",
                        scientific = FALSE)

report <- list(
  folds = sprintf("%s, k = %d, %d by %d blocks of %s by %s m (asked for %s m)",
                  folds$method, folds$k, folds$params$grid_nx,
                  folds$params$grid_ny, m(folds$params$block_width),
                  m(folds$params$block_height), m(folds$params$block_size)),
  score = sprintf("RMSE %.2f (per fold %.2f to %.2f), R2 %.3f",
                  cv$overall$RMSE, min(cv$fold_metrics$RMSE),
                  max(cv$fold_metrics$RMSE), cv$overall$R2),
  coverage = sprintf(paste("%d of %d folds scored, %d rows dropped,",
                           "%d orphan, %d unknown id"),
                     cv$n_folds_succeeded, cv$n_folds_attempted, cv$n_dropped,
                     length(cv$orphan_rows), cv$n_unknown_ids)
)
mi <- residual_morans_i(fit)
report$residuals <- sprintf("Moran's I %.3f (z = %.1f, p = %.3g, %s null)",
                            mi$observed, mi$z, mi$p_value, mi$null)
surface <- predict_surface(fit, n_cells = 1500, covariates = pts,
                           boundary = counties)
aoa <- area_of_applicability(surface, model = fit, folds = folds)
report$applicability <- sprintf("%d of %d grid points outside (DI > %.3f)",
                                aoa$n_outside, aoa$n_new, aoa$threshold)
sac <- estimate_sac_range(pts, "z")
edge <- min(folds$params$block_width, folds$params$block_height)
report$range <- sprintf(paste("estimated range %s m against a narrowest",
                              "block edge of %s m"),
                        m(signif(sac, 2)), m(edge))
for (line in names(report)) say(line, ": ", report[[line]])
## - folds: block_kfold, k = 5, 7 by 2 blocks of 105,579 by 132,408 m (asked
##   for 100,000 m)
## - score: RMSE 2.25 (per fold 1.97 to 2.61), R2 -0.063
## - coverage: 5 of 5 folds scored, 0 rows dropped, 0 orphan, 0 unknown id
## - residuals: Moran's I 0.567 (z = 12.6, p = 3.62e-36, randomisation null)
## - applicability: 0 of 937 grid points outside (DI > 0.073)
## - range: estimated range 280,000 m against a narrowest block edge of
##   105,579 m

The folds line leaves out the CRS; st_crs(pts)$wkt gives it in full, and a layer written with st_write() carries it.

Two lines show a failed model. The cross-validated R² of -0.063 is below zero: the trend surface predicts the held-out blocks worse than the mean of each fold’s training rows does. Moran’s I of 0.57 on the residuals (z = 12.6) says why: most of the structure in z is the field, and a plane in the coordinates cannot represent it. At that point you fit a spatial model rather than report this one; vignette("models") compares the backends.

The narrowest block edge is 105,579 m and the estimated range about 280,000 m, so the blocks are narrower than the range, and a held-out point is still correlated with nearby training data. Whether that makes the score optimistic depends on how far the map’s grid points sit from the data. fold_separation() compares the two against the grid points of the surface above and reads farther: the held-out points sit farther from their training data than the grid points do, so the score tends to read high for this map; narrower blocks, or make_folds(method = "knndm", prediction_points = surface), match it. vignette("spatial-cross-validation") explains the four readings.

The applicability line reads 0 of 937 here because predict_surface() joined the covariate from the nearest observation, so every grid point carries an elev value from a training row. With predictor values sampled from a real covariate raster it need not be zero; vignette("models") covers what to do when it is not. n_cells = 1500 asks for about 1,500 grid points over the bounding box of the data, and boundary = counties keeps the 937 inside the state.

aoa$aoa is the surface with the DI and AOA columns added, so writing it out keeps each point’s flag beside its prediction:

st_write(aoa$aoa, file.path(dir, "surface.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)

What each line is for

Line From Because
folds folds$method, folds$k, folds$params A cross-validated score is the error at the distance the folds put between held-out points and their training data (Milà et al. 2022), so a reader needs the fold geometry to know which map the score describes.
score cv$overall, cv$fold_metrics The pooled score cannot tell a model that fails in one block from one with the same error in every block; the range over folds can. plot_cv_metrics() draws it.
coverage cv$n_folds_succeeded, cv$n_folds_attempted, cv$n_dropped, cv$orphan_rows, cv$n_unknown_ids A score over the folds that ran describes those rows only. The run warns about it, but the warning ends with the session; these fields carry it into the report.
residuals residual_morans_i() Checks whether the model captured the spatial structure in the response; a high I means it did not.
applicability area_of_applicability() A fitted model returns a number everywhere, including ground nothing like its training data, and the cross-validated score does not apply there (Meyer and Pebesma 2021).
range estimate_sac_range(), folds$params, fold_separation() Blocks narrower than the range leave held-out points correlated with their training data; fold_separation() says what that means for the map.
interval coverage, for a model with intervals; not in this report cv_bayes(), plot_calibration() Point predictions can be accurate while their intervals are too narrow or too wide (Heaton et al. 2019 compare both), so RMSE alone can prefer the model whose uncertainty is wrong.

What to save

To rerun the analysis, save:

  • folds$params (the seed, block size, grid and CRS of the folds) and the fold assignment, folds$assignment. Pass make_folds() a seed: without one, folds$params$seed is NULL and the folds differ on every call.
  • For the package’s own fitters, the fit’s $info, which records the settings of the fit; a learner you write yourself records only what it puts there.
  • The cells, with ensure_stable_poly_id() applied, as a GeoPackage.
  • The summary of cell values as an R object, or the report lines written from it. Its three records are attributes, and st_write() writes only columns.
  • The package versions (sessionInfo() in your own script).
st_write(vals, file.path(dir, "cell-values.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
saveRDS(vals, file.path(dir, "cell-values.rds"))

records <- c("pooled", "count_rule", "intervals")
kept <- function(x) sum(records %in% names(attributes(x)))
c(GeoPackage = kept(st_read(file.path(dir, "cell-values.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)),
  RDS        = kept(readRDS(file.path(dir, "cell-values.rds"))))
## GeoPackage        RDS 
##          0          3

Functions that take a seed

These are the exported functions with a seed argument, and its default:

Function Argument Default
get_voronoi_seeds() set_seed NULL
make_folds() seed NULL
voronoi_seeds_random() set_seed NULL
area_of_applicability() seed 123
compare_models_cv() seed 123
cv_bayes() seed 123
cv_block_size_sweep() seed 123
cv_gwr() seed 123
cv_rf() seed 123
cv_spatial() seed 123
determine_optimal_levels() set_seed 123
estimate_sac_range() seed 123
fit_bayesian_spatial_model() seed 123
fit_rf_model() seed 123
kriging_adequacy() seed 123
resolution_profile() seed 123
select_features_forward() seed 123
voronoi_seeds_kmeans() set_seed 456

get_voronoi_seeds(), make_folds() and voronoi_seeds_random() default to NULL and draw from the session’s random stream, so two calls differ unless you pass a seed or call set.seed() first. The others fix a seed by default.

The IDs need no seed. A tessellation’s cell_id does not depend on the order of the input points, and ensure_stable_poly_id() gives the same IDs in any projection (see IDs that survive a reprojection).

The cells themselves are the one output that cannot be regenerated from the others without care. The Voronoi cells of the pooled values come from resolution_profile(), which fits its centres under seed (123 by default; attr(vals, "count_rule") records it), and get_voronoi_seeds() given the selection returns those centres. Given a bare number, get_voronoi_seeds() draws from the session’s random stream unless you pass set_seed. Even a seeded rerun matches only under the same package version, so save the layer.

This article relied on ?assign_features_to_polygons, ?ensure_stable_poly_id, ?summarize_by_cell, ?cell_values_at, ?cv_spatial, ?residual_morans_i, ?area_of_applicability, ?estimate_sac_range and ?fold_separation. vignette("glossary") defines the terms it uses.
